topics.title: fs: Reading and Writing Files
topics.summary: The fs module offers synchronous, callback and promise APIs; prefer fs/promises in application code.
topics.description:
The **`fs`** module talks to the file system. Every operation comes in three styles.

| Style | Example | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous | `fs.readFileSync(p, 'utf8')` | Start-up scripts, CLIs, config loading |
| Callback | `fs.readFile(p, 'utf8', cb)` | Legacy code |
| Promise | `await fs.promises.readFile(p, 'utf8')` | Servers and everything modern |

Import the promise version with `import fs from 'node:fs/promises'`.

### Common operations
* `readFile`, `writeFile` (overwrites), `appendFile`
* `copyFile`, `rename`, `unlink` (delete a file), `rm` (delete files or folders)
* `access`, `stat` to check existence, size and type
* Without an encoding, `readFile` returns a **Buffer**; pass `'utf8'` to get a string

### Why not sync in a server?
Sync calls block the event loop: while one request waits for the disk, every other request freezes. Use them only before the server starts listening.

### Errors
Failures throw errors with a `code` such as `ENOENT` (not found), `EACCES` (permission), `EEXIST` or `EISDIR`. Always handle them:
`try { ... } catch (err) { if (err.code === 'ENOENT') ... }`

### Checking existence
Avoid `exists` followed by read (race condition). Just try the operation and handle `ENOENT`.

### Large files
`readFile` loads the whole file into memory. For big files use streams (see the streams topic) so memory stays flat.

### Paths
Relative paths are resolved against `process.cwd()`, not the file's location. Build absolute paths with `path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'file.txt')`.
keyPoints: Three styles: sync, callback and promise; prefer node:fs/promises
Without an encoding you get a Buffer, with 'utf8' you get a string
Do not use sync methods inside request handlers
Handle error.code values such as ENOENT and EACCES
Use streams for large files
pitfalls: Relative paths that depend on where the process was started
Calling existsSync then reading (race condition) instead of handling ENOENT
Reading multi-GB files with readFile and running out of memory

examples.explanation: Save as .mjs. stat returns size in bytes and type checks.

examples.title: Same thing in the three styles
examples.explanation: Always check the err argument first in the callback style.

interview.q: Why should you avoid fs.readFileSync in a web server?
interview.a: It blocks the single JavaScript thread until the disk read finishes, so no other request can be handled meanwhile. Use fs.promises (non-blocking) inside handlers; sync calls are fine at start-up.

interview.q: How do you check whether a file exists?
interview.a: Prefer to try the operation and catch ENOENT, because checking first with exists/access can race with other processes. fs.access or fs.stat in a try/catch also works when you only need the check.

topics.title: fs: Directories, Streams and Watching
topics.summary: List and create folders, walk trees recursively, stream big files and react to changes with fs.watch.
topics.description:
### Directories
* `fs.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` creates nested folders and does not fail if they exist
* `fs.readdir(dir)` returns names; `{ withFileTypes: true }` returns `Dirent` objects with `isFile()` and `isDirectory()`
* `fs.readdir(dir, { recursive: true })` lists the whole tree (Node 20+)
* `fs.rm(path, { recursive: true, force: true })` is `rm -rf`
* `fs.mkdtemp(prefix)` makes a unique temporary folder
* `fs.glob(pattern)` finds files by pattern in current Node versions

### Metadata
`fs.stat` gives `size`, `mtime`, `birthtime`, `mode`, `isFile()`, `isDirectory()`. `fs.lstat` does not follow symlinks.

### Streams for big files
`fs.createReadStream(file)` and `fs.createWriteStream(file)` move data in 64 KB chunks, so memory usage stays small. Combine with `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises` to copy or transform (compress, parse) safely.

### Watching for changes
`fs.watch(path)` emits events when a file or folder changes. It is the foundation of `node --watch`, nodemon and dev servers. Behaviour differs per OS (duplicate events are common), so debounce them. In ESM you can iterate: `for await (const e of fs.promises.watch(dir))`.

### File handles
`const fh = await fs.open(path, 'r+')` gives low-level control (read at an offset, write at a position). Always `await fh.close()` in a `finally` block, or use `await using` where available.

### Permissions
`fs.chmod`, `fs.access(path, fs.constants.R_OK)` check/set permission bits (mostly meaningful on Linux and macOS).
keyPoints: mkdir recursive and rm recursive replace shell mkdir -p / rm -rf
readdir with withFileTypes avoids an extra stat per entry
createReadStream/createWriteStream keep memory flat for big files
fs.watch fires duplicate events: debounce them
Close file handles in finally
pitfalls: Deleting with rm recursive and force on an unvalidated user-supplied path
Assuming fs.watch events are one per change
Forgetting to close FileHandles (descriptor leaks)

examples.title: Walk a directory tree
examples.explanation: An async generator makes recursive traversal lazy and easy to consume.

examples.title: Watch a folder
examples.explanation: The AbortController is the clean way to stop a watcher.

interview.q: How do you copy a 5 GB file without exhausting memory?
interview.a: Use fs.createReadStream piped into fs.createWriteStream (via stream.pipeline), or fs.copyFile which delegates to the OS. Both avoid loading the whole file into memory.

interview.q: Why does fs.watch sometimes fire twice?
interview.a: Editors and operating systems emit several low-level events (truncate then write, temp file then rename) for one save. Debounce events for a few milliseconds and compare file contents or mtime.

topics.title: path Module
topics.summary: Build, parse and normalise file paths in a cross-platform way with path.join, resolve, basename, extname and friends.
topics.description:
Never build paths by string concatenation (`dir + '/' + file`). Windows uses `\` and Linux/macOS use `/`. The **`path`** module handles the difference for you.

### Most used functions
| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `path.join(...parts)` | Join and normalise segments |
| `path.resolve(...parts)` | Produce an **absolute** path, processing right to left until one is absolute; starts from `process.cwd()` |
| `path.basename(p, ext?)` | Last part (file name) |
| `path.dirname(p)` | Folder part |
| `path.extname(p)` | Extension including the dot |
| `path.parse(p)` / `path.format(obj)` | Split into `{ root, dir, base, name, ext }` and back |
| `path.normalize(p)` | Collapse `..`, `.` and double slashes |
| `path.relative(from, to)` | Relative path between two places |
| `path.isAbsolute(p)` | Boolean |
| `path.sep`, `path.delimiter` | `/` or `\`, and `:` or `;` |

### join vs resolve
* `join` simply glues and cleans: `join('a', 'b')` is `a/b`
* `resolve` always returns an absolute path: `resolve('a', 'b')` is `<cwd>/a/b`

### posix and win32
`path.posix` and `path.win32` force one style regardless of the OS. Use `path.posix` for URLs and archive paths.

### Security: path traversal
When joining user input to a base folder, a value like `../../etc/passwd` can escape it. After resolving, check that the result still starts with the base folder.
keyPoints: Use path.join/resolve instead of string concatenation
resolve returns an absolute path, join does not
path.parse splits a path into root, dir, base, name and ext
Validate that joined user input stays inside the intended base directory
pitfalls: Hard-coding / or \ separators
Trusting user supplied file names (path traversal)
Using relative paths that depend on process.cwd()

examples.title: Everyday path helpers (POSIX output)
examples.explanation: On Windows the separators in the output will be backslashes.

examples.title: Prevent path traversal
examples.explanation: Always compare against the resolved base plus a separator.

interview.q: Difference between path.join and path.resolve?
interview.a: join concatenates segments with the platform separator and normalises the result (may stay relative). resolve builds an absolute path, working from right to left and falling back to the current working directory.

interview.q: What is path traversal and how do you stop it?
interview.a: An attack that uses ../ sequences in user input to read files outside the intended directory. Resolve the final path and verify it starts with the allowed base directory, or use an allow-list of file names.

topics.title: os Module
topics.summary: Read information about the machine: CPUs, memory, platform, hostname, home and temp directories.
topics.description:
The **`os`** module exposes details about the operating system and hardware. It is useful for diagnostics, choosing worker counts and writing cross-platform tools.

### Frequent members
| Member | Returns |
|---|---|
| `os.platform()` | `'linux'`, `'darwin'`, `'win32'` |
| `os.arch()` | `'x64'`, `'arm64'` |
| `os.cpus()` | Array with one entry per logical core |
| `os.availableParallelism()` | Number of threads you should use (respects container limits better than `cpus().length`) |
| `os.totalmem()` / `os.freemem()` | Memory in bytes |
| `os.homedir()` | User home directory |
| `os.tmpdir()` | Temp directory |
| `os.hostname()` | Machine name |
| `os.uptime()` | Seconds since boot |
| `os.loadavg()` | 1, 5 and 15 minute load (always zeros on Windows) |
| `os.networkInterfaces()` | IP addresses |
| `os.EOL` | Line ending: `\n` or `\r\n` |
| `os.userInfo()` | Current user |

### When to use
* Sizing a `cluster` or worker pool: `os.availableParallelism()`
* Storing cache files: `path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'myapp')`
* Platform specific behaviour: `if (os.platform() === 'win32') ...`
* Health endpoints that report free memory

### Containers note
Inside Docker or Kubernetes, `os.totalmem()` returns the **host** memory, not the container limit. Use `process.constrainedMemory()` or read the cgroup files for real limits.
keyPoints: os reports platform, CPUs, memory, directories and network info
Use os.availableParallelism() to size worker pools
Use os.tmpdir() and os.homedir() instead of hard-coded paths
Memory values are in bytes and may show host values in containers
pitfalls: Hard-coding C:\\temp or /tmp
Trusting os.totalmem() inside containers
Writing \n manually in files meant for Windows tools instead of os.EOL

examples.title: System report
examples.explanation: Output differs per machine.

interview.q: How do you find how many worker processes to start?
interview.a: Use os.availableParallelism() (or os.cpus().length on older Node). It gives the number of logical CPUs that can run in parallel and is container-aware.

interview.q: Why use os.EOL?
interview.a: Windows uses \r\n and Unix uses \n for line breaks. os.EOL gives the right one for the current platform when generating text files.

topics.title: URL and URLSearchParams
topics.summary: Parse, build and modify URLs and query strings safely with the WHATWG URL classes.
topics.description:
Do not split URLs with regular expressions. Use the standard **`URL`** and **`URLSearchParams`** classes (global in Node, same as in browsers).

### Parsing
`new URL('https://user:pw@example.com:8080/a/b?x=1#top')` gives:
* `protocol` `https:`, `host` `example.com:8080`, `hostname`, `port`
* `pathname` `/a/b`, `search` `?x=1`, `hash` `#top`
* `origin`, `href`, `username`, `password`

An invalid URL throws `TypeError` (`ERR_INVALID_URL`), so wrap user input in try/catch. `URL.canParse(str)` checks without throwing.

### Relative URLs
`new URL('../img/a.png', 'https://site.com/blog/post/')` resolves against a base.

### Query strings
`url.searchParams` is a live `URLSearchParams`:
* `get`, `getAll`, `has`, `append`, `set`, `delete`
* Iterable: `for (const [k, v] of params)`
* `toString()` encodes spaces as `+` and special characters safely
* `Object.fromEntries(params)` converts to a plain object (last duplicate wins)

### In an HTTP server
`req.url` is just the path and query (`/search?q=node`). Combine with a base to parse: `new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost')`.

### File URLs
`import.meta.url` is a `file://` URL. Convert with `fileURLToPath(url)` and `pathToFileURL(path)` from `node:url`.

### Legacy API
`url.parse()` and the `querystring` module are legacy. Avoid them for new code.
keyPoints: Use new URL() instead of manual parsing
searchParams handles encoding and repeated keys
Pass a base URL when parsing req.url or relative links
fileURLToPath converts import.meta.url to a path
URL.canParse validates safely
pitfalls: Forgetting that new URL throws on invalid input
Using the legacy url.parse
Concatenating query strings by hand without encoding

examples.explanation: This particular example is plain JavaScript and works in any runtime.

examples.title: Parsing req.url in a server
examples.explanation: GET /search?q=node returns {"path":"/search","q":"node"}.

interview.q: How do you read query parameters in plain Node?
interview.a: Create a URL from req.url with a base such as http://localhost, then use url.searchParams.get('name'). Express exposes the same data as req.query.

interview.q: What does URLSearchParams do for you?
interview.a: It parses, builds and percent-encodes query strings correctly, supports repeated keys and iteration, and is available in both Node and browsers.

topics.title: util: promisify, inspect, parseArgs
topics.summary: util bundles helpers: promisify callback APIs, deep-print objects, parse CLI flags, format strings and check types.
topics.description:
The **`util`** module is a toolbox of small helpers.

### util.promisify
Turns an error-first callback function into one that returns a promise:
`const sleep = util.promisify(setTimeout)`. Many core APIs already have promise versions, but older libraries do not.
Opposite: `util.callbackify`.

### util.inspect
What `console.log` uses internally. Options: `depth` (default 2, `null` = unlimited), `colors`, `compact`, `breakLength`, `showHidden`. Define `[util.inspect.custom]` on a class to control how it prints. `console.dir(obj, { depth: null })` is the shortcut.

### util.parseArgs
Parses command line arguments without a dependency (stable since Node 20). Declare `options` with `type` (`string` or `boolean`), `short` aliases, `default` and `multiple`. Positional arguments need `allowPositionals: true`.

### util.format
printf-style formatting: `%s` string, `%d` number, `%i` integer, `%j` JSON, `%o`/`%O` objects, `%%` percent.

### util.styleText
Adds terminal colours without a library: `util.styleText('green', 'OK')`.

### util.types and util.isDeepStrictEqual
`util.types.isPromise(x)`, `isRegExp`, `isDate`. `util.isDeepStrictEqual(a, b)` compares objects by value.

### util.deprecate
Wrap an old function to print a one-time warning when it is called.

### util.TextEncoder / TextDecoder
Convert strings to UTF-8 bytes and back.

### util.debuglog
Logs only when `NODE_DEBUG=name` is set, ideal for library diagnostics.
keyPoints: promisify converts callback APIs to promises
inspect with depth null prints nested objects fully
parseArgs replaces small CLI parsing libraries
format, styleText, deprecate and isDeepStrictEqual are handy extras
pitfalls: Promisifying a function that does not follow the (err, value) callback convention
Reading truncated console.log output and forgetting that depth defaults to 2

examples.title: promisify and inspect
examples.explanation: console.log hides objects deeper than 2 levels.

examples.title: parseArgs CLI
examples.explanation: Unknown flags throw an error by default, which is usually what you want.

interview.q: What does util.promisify do?
interview.a: It wraps a function whose last argument is an error-first callback (err, result) and returns a new function that returns a promise resolving with the result or rejecting with the error.

interview.q: How do you print a deeply nested object in full?
interview.a: Use util.inspect(obj, { depth: null }) or console.dir(obj, { depth: null }); the default depth of 2 replaces deeper levels with [Object].

topics.title: events: EventEmitter
topics.summary: The observer pattern at the heart of Node: on, once, emit, error events and the memory leak warning.
topics.description:
Much of Node (streams, servers, processes) is built on **`EventEmitter`**. An emitter lets objects announce that something happened and lets other code react.

### Core API
* `emitter.on(name, listener)` (alias `addListener`) subscribes
* `emitter.once(name, listener)` runs only the first time
* `emitter.emit(name, ...args)` calls all listeners **synchronously**, in the order they were added, and returns `true` if there were any
* `emitter.off(name, listener)` / `removeAllListeners(name)` unsubscribes
* `emitter.prependListener` runs a listener first
* `listenerCount(name)`, `eventNames()`

### The special `'error'` event
If an emitter emits `'error'` and **no listener** exists, Node throws and the process crashes. Always attach an error listener to emitters you create (streams, sockets).

### Making your own emitter
Extend the class: `class Chat extends EventEmitter {}`. This is how you build decoupled modules such as job queues, loggers or game engines.

### Waiting for an event
`await once(emitter, 'ready')` (from `node:events`) turns an event into a promise. `on(emitter, 'data')` gives an async iterator.

### Memory leak warning
More than 10 listeners for one event prints `MaxListenersExceededWarning`. It usually means you add listeners inside a loop or request handler without removing them. Raise it with `setMaxListeners` only when it is intentional.

### Sync vs async
`emit` is synchronous. If a listener is slow it blocks the emitter. Use `setImmediate` or queue work inside the listener for heavy tasks.

### EventTarget
Browsers use `EventTarget` and `addEventListener`; Node supports it too, but EventEmitter remains the standard in Node APIs.
keyPoints: on/once subscribe, emit triggers listeners synchronously in order
An unhandled 'error' event crashes the process
Extend EventEmitter to create your own event-driven classes
events.once() converts an event into a promise
MaxListenersExceededWarning hints at leaked listeners
pitfalls: Registering listeners inside a loop or per-request without removing them
Emitting 'error' without a listener
Assuming listeners run asynchronously

examples.explanation: The once listener runs only for the first order.

placing 1

interview.q: Is EventEmitter synchronous or asynchronous?
interview.a: emit() calls the listeners synchronously in registration order before it returns. The listeners themselves can start async work, but the dispatch is synchronous.

interview.q: What happens if you emit 'error' without a listener?
interview.a: Node throws the error as an uncaught exception, which crashes the process, so you should always register an 'error' listener on emitters.

topics.title: Buffer and Binary Data
topics.summary: Buffers hold raw bytes; learn creation, encodings (utf8, hex, base64), slicing and when you meet them.
topics.description:
A **Buffer** is a fixed-size chunk of memory holding raw bytes. It is a subclass of `Uint8Array` and is used for files, network packets, images, encryption and anything that is not plain text.

### Creating buffers
* `Buffer.from('hello')` from a string (UTF-8 by default)
* `Buffer.from([104, 105])` from bytes
* `Buffer.from(str, 'base64' | 'hex')` decoding
* `Buffer.alloc(10)` zero-filled, **safe**
* `Buffer.allocUnsafe(10)` faster, may contain old memory (never send it to clients unless fully overwritten)
* `Buffer.concat([a, b])`

### Converting
`buf.toString('utf8' | 'hex' | 'base64' | 'base64url')`. Example: `Buffer.from('hello').toString('base64')` is `aGVsbG8=`.

### Length is bytes, not characters
`'héllo'.length` is 5 but `Buffer.from('héllo').length` is 6, because `é` takes two bytes in UTF-8. Remember this for `Content-Length` headers and limits.

### Reading and writing numbers
`buf.readUInt32BE(0)`, `buf.writeInt16LE(-2, 4)`; BE/LE is big or little endian. Used when speaking binary protocols.

### Other helpers
* `buf.slice` / `subarray` share memory with the original (no copy)
* `buf.equals(other)`, `Buffer.compare`, `buf.indexOf`
* `Buffer.byteLength(str)` counts bytes without allocating
* Indexing `buf[0]` gives a byte (0-255)

### Where you meet them
`fs.readFile` without an encoding, stream `data` events, `crypto` outputs, and HTTP request bodies.
keyPoints: Buffer is raw bytes and a Uint8Array subclass
Convert with toString(encoding) and Buffer.from(string, encoding)
Length counts bytes, not characters
Prefer Buffer.alloc over allocUnsafe
subarray shares memory instead of copying
pitfalls: Using string.length as the byte size of UTF-8 text
Concatenating chunks with + (corrupts multi-byte characters); collect and Buffer.concat instead
Using allocUnsafe and leaking old memory content

examples.title: Buffer basics
examples.explanation: 258 is 0x0102 so the first four bytes are 00 00 01 02.

interview.q: Difference between Buffer.alloc and Buffer.allocUnsafe?
interview.a: alloc returns zero-filled memory. allocUnsafe skips zeroing for speed, so it can expose old data from memory; use it only when you immediately overwrite every byte.

interview.q: Why is string.length not equal to buffer.length?
interview.a: string.length counts UTF-16 code units, while buffer length counts bytes in the chosen encoding. Non-ASCII characters take 2-4 bytes in UTF-8.

topics.title: crypto: Hashing, HMAC and Random Values
topics.summary: Create hashes, HMAC signatures, random tokens, UUIDs and encrypt data; know when to use bcrypt or argon2 instead.
topics.description:
The **`crypto`** module wraps OpenSSL for security tasks.

### Hashing
`crypto.createHash('sha256').update(data).digest('hex')`. A hash is one-way and always gives the same output for the same input. Use SHA-256 or SHA-512 for checksums and fingerprints. **MD5 and SHA-1 are broken** for security.

### HMAC
`crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(data).digest('hex')` produces a hash that also proves the sender knew the **secret key**. It is used for webhook signatures, signed cookies and JWT HS256. Compare signatures with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` to avoid timing attacks.

### Random values
* `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')` for tokens, secrets and salts
* `crypto.randomUUID()` for a v4 UUID
* `crypto.randomInt(1, 100)` for an unbiased random integer
* **Never** use `Math.random()` for anything security related

### Passwords
Plain hashes are too fast for passwords. Use a slow, salted algorithm:
* Built in: `crypto.scrypt` / `scryptSync(password, salt, 64)`
* Libraries: **bcrypt** or **argon2** (best choice today)

### Encryption
Symmetric: `createCipheriv('aes-256-gcm', key, iv)` (use a fresh 12-byte IV per message and store the auth tag). Asymmetric: `generateKeyPairSync('rsa' | 'ed25519')`, `sign`, `verify`.

### Web Crypto
`globalThis.crypto.subtle` offers the browser-compatible API, and `crypto.getRandomValues` works everywhere.
keyPoints: createHash for checksums, createHmac for keyed signatures
Use randomBytes/randomUUID/randomInt, never Math.random, for secrets
Passwords need slow salted hashing: scrypt, bcrypt or argon2
Compare secrets with timingSafeEqual
MD5 and SHA-1 are not secure
pitfalls: Storing passwords with plain SHA-256
Reusing an IV (nonce) with AES-GCM
Comparing signatures with === (timing attack)

examples.explanation: Hash and HMAC outputs are deterministic; random values change on each run.

examples.title: Password hashing with scrypt
examples.explanation: In real projects most teams use the bcrypt or argon2 package for the same job.

interview.q: Why not store passwords with SHA-256?
interview.a: SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second. Password hashes must be slow, salted and tunable (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2).

interview.q: Hash vs HMAC?
interview.a: A hash only depends on the data, so anyone can compute it. An HMAC mixes in a secret key, so only parties with the key can create or verify it; it proves integrity and authenticity.

topics.title: zlib: Compression
topics.summary: Compress and decompress data with gzip, deflate and brotli, in memory or as streams.
topics.description:
**`zlib`** compresses data using gzip, deflate or brotli. Compression saves bandwidth and disk space, especially for text (JSON, HTML, logs) which often shrinks by 70-90%.

### Three APIs
1. **Sync**: `zlib.gzipSync(buf)` / `gunzipSync` for small data
2. **Async/callback** or promisified: `gzip(buf, cb)`
3. **Streams**: `zlib.createGzip()` / `createGunzip()` for large files and HTTP

### Algorithms
| Format | Functions | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| gzip | `gzip`, `gunzip` | Most common (files, HTTP) |
| deflate | `deflate`, `inflate` | Raw zlib format |
| brotli | `brotliCompress`, `brotliDecompress` | Better ratio, standard for HTTPS text |

### Streaming a file
`pipeline(createReadStream('big.log'), createGzip(), createWriteStream('big.log.gz'))` keeps memory constant.

### HTTP compression
Browsers send `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br`. A server can compress responses and add `Content-Encoding: gzip`. In real apps use the `compression` middleware or let nginx/CDN do it.

### Levels
`{ level: 9 }` is smallest but slowest; `level: 1` is fastest. Default (6) is a good balance.

### Security: zip bombs
A tiny input can expand to gigabytes. When decompressing untrusted data set `maxOutputLength`.

### CPU note
Compression is CPU-intensive. Sync versions block the event loop; the async ones use the thread pool.
keyPoints: zlib supports gzip, deflate and brotli
Use streams (createGzip) for big files and HTTP bodies
Text compresses very well; images and videos do not
Limit output size when decompressing untrusted input
pitfalls: Using gzipSync on large data inside a request handler
Double-compressing already compressed files (jpg, zip)
Forgetting the Content-Encoding header when sending compressed bodies

examples.title: Compress in memory and as a stream
examples.explanation: Repeated text compresses extremely well.

interview.q: How do you compress an HTTP response in Node?
interview.a: Check the Accept-Encoding header, pipe the response body through zlib.createGzip() (or brotli), and set Content-Encoding. Usually the compression middleware or a reverse proxy does this.

interview.q: Why is the sync zlib API risky on servers?
interview.a: It runs on the main thread, blocking the event loop during compression. The async and stream APIs run on the libuv thread pool.

topics.title: child_process
topics.summary: Run shell commands and other programs from Node with exec, execFile, spawn and fork.
topics.description:
**`child_process`** starts other programs from your script (git, ffmpeg, python, another Node file).

| Function | Best for | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `exec(cmd, cb)` | Short shell commands, small output | Buffered string |
| `execFile(file, args, cb)` | Run a program **without a shell** (safer) | Buffered |
| `spawn(cmd, args)` | Long running or large output | Streams (`stdout`, `stderr`) |
| `fork(modulePath)` | Another **Node** script with an IPC message channel | `send()` / `on('message')` |
| `execSync`, `spawnSync` | Scripts and build tools | Blocking |

### Promises
`const { promisify } = require('node:util'); const execP = promisify(exec);` returns `{ stdout, stderr }`.

### spawn in detail
`const child = spawn('ls', ['-la'])` gives `child.stdout.on('data', ...)`, `child.on('close', code => ...)` and `child.kill()`. Options: `cwd`, `env`, `stdio: 'inherit'` (pass through to your terminal), `shell: true`.

### Exit codes and errors
A non-zero exit code is a failure. `'error'` fires if the program cannot start (not found). `exec` rejects with an error that has `code`, `stdout` and `stderr`.

### Security: command injection
Building a command string such as `"git log " + userInput` lets a user inject `; rm -rf /`. Never put untrusted data in a shell string. Use `execFile` or `spawn` with an arguments **array** and `shell: false`.

### fork vs worker_threads
`fork` creates a whole new process with its own memory (heavier, isolated). `worker_threads` shares the process and is lighter for CPU work.

interview.q: exec vs spawn?
interview.a: exec runs a command in a shell and buffers all output until it finishes (limited by maxBuffer), so it suits short commands. spawn streams stdout/stderr as data arrives and avoids the shell by default, so it suits long-running or large-output programs.

interview.q: How do you avoid command injection?
interview.a: Never interpolate user input into a shell string. Use execFile or spawn with the program and an array of arguments, without shell: true, and validate input against an allow-list.

topics.title: readline: Interactive Input
topics.summary: Read user input line by line from the terminal or from a large file.
topics.description:
**`readline`** reads a stream one line at a time. It has two main jobs: interactive prompts in CLI tools and processing big text files line by line.

### Prompting the user
With `node:readline/promises`:
`const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout }); const name = await rl.question('Name? '); rl.close();`

Always call `rl.close()`, otherwise the process stays alive waiting for input.

### Reading a file line by line
`createInterface({ input: fs.createReadStream('big.csv'), crlfDelay: Infinity })` then `for await (const line of rl)`. Memory stays small even for huge files; this is the standard way to parse logs and CSV.

### Events
* `'line'` for each line
* `'close'` at the end of input or Ctrl+C / Ctrl+D
* `rl.on('SIGINT')` to customise Ctrl+C

### Other helpers
* `readline.clearLine`, `cursorTo`, `moveCursor` for progress bars
* `rl.setPrompt('> ')` and `rl.prompt()` build a REPL-like loop
* Piped input works: `echo "Ann" | node ask.mjs`

### For rich CLIs
Libraries such as `inquirer`, `prompts` and `@clack/prompts` add menus, checkboxes and validation on top of the same idea.

### Windows line endings
Use `crlfDelay: Infinity` so `\r\n` counts as a single line break.

for await over the interface reads large files line by line
Close the interface or the process will not exit

Reading an entire large file into memory when line streaming would do

interview.q: How do you process a 10 GB log file in Node?
interview.a: Stream it with fs.createReadStream and wrap it in readline.createInterface, then iterate lines with for await. Only a small buffer is in memory at any time.

interview.q: Why does my script hang after reading input?
interview.a: The readline interface keeps stdin open. Call rl.close() when you are done so the event loop has nothing left to wait for.

topics.title: Timers: setTimeout, setImmediate, timers/promises
topics.summary: Schedule work with setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate and process.nextTick, and use the promise timers.
topics.description:
Node provides the familiar browser timers plus a few extras.

| API | Runs |
|---|---|
| `setTimeout(fn, ms)` | After at least `ms` milliseconds |
| `setInterval(fn, ms)` | Repeatedly every `ms` |
| `setImmediate(fn)` | After the current I/O phase (check phase of the event loop) |
| `process.nextTick(fn)` | Before anything else, right after the current operation |
| `queueMicrotask(fn)` | In the microtask queue (like promise callbacks) |

### Timer objects
In Node, `setTimeout` returns a `Timeout` object, not a number. Methods: `clearTimeout(t)`, `t.unref()` (do not keep the process alive for this timer), `t.ref()`, `t.refresh()`.

### Not exact
The delay is a **minimum**. If the event loop is busy the callback runs later. Never use timers for precise timing.

### Promise timers
`import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises'` gives `await sleep(1000)`, and supports an `AbortSignal`. `setInterval` there is an async iterator.

### Clearing
Always clear intervals you no longer need, or the process never exits. Using `unref()` on a background interval (metrics, cleanup) lets Node exit when real work is done.

### Zero delay
`setTimeout(fn, 0)` actually becomes 1 ms. Compared to `setImmediate`, the order is not guaranteed in the main module but is always immediate-first inside an I/O callback (see the event loop topic).

### Long delays
Delays above 2,147,483,647 ms (about 24.8 days) overflow and fire immediately.

unref() lets the process exit despite an active timer

examples.explanation: The script ends right after done because the unref'd interval does not block exit.

interview.q: Is setTimeout(fn, 100) guaranteed to run after exactly 100ms?
interview.a: No. 100 ms is the minimum delay. The callback is queued once the time elapsed, but runs only when the event loop is free, so it can be late if other work is running.

interview.q: What does timer.unref() do?
interview.a: It tells Node not to wait for this timer before exiting. If only unref'd timers remain, the process ends. Useful for housekeeping tasks.

topics.title: assert and Validating Assumptions
topics.summary: node:assert provides strict equality, deep equality and throws checks used by tests and defensive code.
topics.description:
**`assert`** throws an `AssertionError` when a condition is false. It is the base of `node:test` and a good way to check assumptions in scripts.

### Use the strict mode
Import from `node:assert/strict` (or `assert.strict`). Then `equal` means `===` and `deepEqual` means strict deep comparison. The loose versions use `==` and cause surprising passes (`1 == '1'`).

### Main functions
| Function | Checks |
|---|---|
| `assert.ok(value)` / `assert(value)` | Truthy |
| `assert.equal(a, b)` | `a === b` (strict mode) |
| `assert.notEqual(a, b)` | Not equal |
| `assert.deepEqual(a, b)` | Objects/arrays equal by value |
| `assert.throws(fn, expected)` | `fn` throws a matching error |
| `assert.rejects(promiseOrFn, expected)` | Promise rejects |
| `assert.match(str, regex)` | String matches regex |
| `assert.fail(message)` | Always fails |

### Custom messages
Last argument: `assert.equal(total, 10, 'cart total should be 10')`. Without it Node prints a helpful diff of actual vs expected.

### Production use?
Use assert for **programmer errors** and invariants during tests and scripts. For validating user input, throw proper errors (400 responses); do not rely on assert, and avoid assert in hot paths.

### Test runner
`node --test` discovers files and runs `node:test`, which uses assert for the checks themselves. See the testing section.

assert.throws and assert.rejects test failing code
AssertionError shows a readable diff
Good for invariants and tests, not for user input validation
pitfalls: Using the legacy loose assert.equal (==)
Forgetting await with assert.rejects
Using assertions to validate request data

examples.explanation: Strict equality treats 1 and "1" as different.

interview.q: assert.equal vs assert.strictEqual?
interview.a: In the legacy mode equal uses ==, strictEqual uses ===. When you import node:assert/strict, equal behaves like strictEqual, which is the recommended setup.

interview.q: How do you assert that an async function fails?
interview.a: Use await assert.rejects(fnOrPromise, expectedError). Without await the assertion may not finish before the test ends.

topics.title: The process Object
topics.summary: process gives access to arguments, environment variables, exit codes, signals, stdin/stdout, memory and uptime.
topics.description:
**`process`** is a global object describing the current Node process.

### Information
* `process.argv`: `[nodePath, scriptPath, ...args]`
* `process.env`: environment variables (all values are strings)
* `process.cwd()`: current working directory; `process.chdir(dir)`
* `process.pid`, `process.platform`, `process.version`, `process.versions`
* `process.uptime()`, `process.memoryUsage()`, `process.cpuUsage()`, `process.hrtime.bigint()`

### Standard streams
`process.stdin`, `process.stdout`, `process.stderr` are streams. `console.log` writes to stdout and `console.error` to stderr. Pipes: `echo hi | node app.js` fills stdin.

### Exiting
* `process.exit(code)` stops immediately; pending async work is lost
* `process.exitCode = 1` sets the code and lets the process end naturally (preferred)
* Exit code 0 = success

### Events
* `'exit'` (sync cleanup only) and `'beforeExit'`
* `'uncaughtException'` and `'unhandledRejection'`: last-resort handlers: log and exit, do not continue
* **Signals**: `'SIGINT'` (Ctrl+C), `'SIGTERM'` (kill, Docker/Kubernetes stop). Handle them for graceful shutdown. (`SIGKILL` cannot be caught.)

### Environment variables
`process.env.PORT ?? 3000`. Values are strings so convert: `Number(process.env.PORT)`. Setting `process.env.X = undefined` stores the string `'undefined'`; use `delete`.

### nextTick
`process.nextTick(fn)` runs before promise microtasks (see the event loop).

### Warnings and loading env files
`process.loadEnvFile('.env')` loads a file at runtime, and `process.emitWarning()` raises warnings.

Prefer process.exitCode over process.exit()

examples.explanation: Setting exitCode lets the exit handler run naturally.

interview.q: process.exit() vs process.exitCode?
interview.a: exit() terminates immediately, possibly dropping pending I/O and timers. Setting exitCode records the code but lets the event loop drain and the process end naturally, which is safer.

interview.q: What are SIGINT and SIGTERM?
interview.a: SIGINT is sent by Ctrl+C, SIGTERM is the polite termination request used by Docker, Kubernetes and process managers. Handle both to close servers and database connections before exiting. SIGKILL cannot be handled.

topics.title: worker_threads
topics.summary: Run CPU-heavy JavaScript on separate threads without blocking the event loop, with message passing and shared memory.
topics.description:
Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so a CPU-heavy loop freezes every request. **`worker_threads`** lets you run JavaScript in parallel **threads** inside the same process.

### Basics
* `new Worker(file, { workerData })` starts a worker
* In the worker: `parentPort.postMessage(result)` and `parentPort.on('message', ...)`
* `isMainThread` tells which side you are in, so one file can contain both
* Events on the worker: `'message'`, `'error'`, `'exit'`

### Communication
Messages are copied with the **structured clone** algorithm (objects, arrays, Maps, typed arrays). To avoid copying large data:
* **Transfer** ownership of an `ArrayBuffer`: `postMessage(buf, [buf])`
* Share memory with `SharedArrayBuffer` and coordinate using `Atomics`

### Workers vs child processes vs cluster
| | worker_threads | child_process / cluster |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Same process, separate heaps | Separate processes |
| Start cost | Lower | Higher |
| Best for | CPU tasks (hashing, image resize, parsing) | Isolation, scaling servers on all cores |

### Not for I/O
Workers do not make database or HTTP calls faster; Node's async I/O is already non-blocking. Use workers only for CPU work.

### Worker pools
Creating a worker per request is expensive (tens of ms). Keep a pool and reuse workers. Libraries: **piscina**, **workerpool**.

### Memory limits
Each worker has its own V8 heap; set `resourceLimits: { maxOldGenerationSizeMb: 256 }`.

Communicate with postMessage (structured clone) or SharedArrayBuffer
Use for CPU-bound work, not I/O
Reuse workers through a pool such as piscina
pitfalls: Spawning a new worker for every request
Sending huge objects back and forth instead of transferring buffers

interview.q: When would you use worker_threads instead of cluster?
interview.a: Use worker_threads to offload CPU-intensive tasks inside one application without blocking the event loop. Use cluster (processes) to run multiple copies of a server so you can use all cores for handling requests.

interview.q: How do workers share data?
interview.a: Via postMessage (data is cloned or ArrayBuffers transferred) or via SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics for true shared memory.

topics.title: cluster
topics.summary: Fork one worker process per CPU core, all sharing the same server port, and restart them when they die.
topics.description:
A Node process uses only **one CPU core** for JavaScript. On an 8-core server you waste seven. The **`cluster`** module starts several copies (workers) of your app that all listen on the **same port**.

### How it works
1. The **primary** process (`cluster.isPrimary`) calls `cluster.fork()` once per core.
2. Each worker is a separate Node process with its own memory, event loop and V8.
3. The primary accepts connections and distributes them to workers (round-robin on Linux/macOS).
4. If a worker crashes, the primary can fork a new one.

### Example outline
`if (cluster.isPrimary) { for (...) cluster.fork(); cluster.on('exit', () => cluster.fork()); } else { http.createServer(...).listen(3000); }`

### Things to remember
* **No shared memory**: in-memory sessions, caches, counters and websockets are per worker. Use Redis or a database for shared state.
* Each worker has its own database connection pool: size pools accordingly.
* Workers communicate via IPC messages (`process.send`).
* Zero-downtime restarts: restart workers one at a time.

### In practice
Most teams do not write cluster code by hand:
* **PM2** has `pm2 start app.js -i max` (cluster mode)
* **Containers**: run one process per container and scale containers horizontally
* **Kubernetes** / load balancers do the distribution

### cluster vs worker_threads
cluster scales **request handling** across cores; worker_threads offloads **CPU tasks**.
keyPoints: cluster forks multiple processes that share one listening port
Primary distributes connections; workers are isolated processes
In-memory state is not shared between workers

Respawn workers on exit

Forking more workers than cores
Not restarting crashed workers

interview.q: Why use cluster?
interview.a: To use all CPU cores: each worker process runs the same server on the shared port, multiplying throughput and adding resilience because a crashed worker can be replaced.

interview.q: What is the main limitation of clustering?
interview.a: Workers do not share memory, so in-process state such as sessions, caches or WebSocket connections must move to external stores like Redis (or use sticky sessions).

topics.title: perf_hooks: Measuring Performance
topics.summary: Measure durations with performance.now, marks and measures, timerify functions and track event loop delay.
topics.description:
The **`perf_hooks`** module (and the global `performance`) gives high resolution timing.

### Quick timing
* `performance.now()` returns milliseconds with microsecond precision since the process started
* `console.time('label')` / `console.timeEnd('label')` is the casual version
* `process.hrtime.bigint()` returns nanoseconds as a BigInt
* `Date.now()` is not suitable for benchmarks because the system clock can jump

### Marks and measures
`performance.mark('start')`, `performance.mark('end')`, `performance.measure('task', 'start', 'end')` record named points and durations. Read them with `performance.getEntriesByName('task')`.

### PerformanceObserver
Listen to entries as they are created, including built-ins such as garbage collection (`'gc'`), HTTP requests, and `'function'` entries produced by `performance.timerify(fn)`.

### Event loop delay
`monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 })` creates a histogram showing how long the loop is blocked. Values (mean, p99, max) reveal blocking code. It is also a great health metric.

`performance.eventLoopUtilization()` returns how busy the loop is (0 to 1).

### When to use
* Compare two algorithm implementations
* Time database queries or external calls and log slow ones
* Expose event loop lag in monitoring dashboards

### Benchmark tips
Run code many times, warm up first (JIT), and use dedicated tools (`mitata`, `tinybench`) for serious comparisons.

interview.q: Why not use Date.now() for benchmarks?
interview.a: It has millisecond resolution and follows the system clock, which can jump when the time syncs. performance.now() and process.hrtime are monotonic and high resolution.

interview.q: What does event loop delay tell you?
interview.a: How late timers fire compared to schedule. High values mean synchronous code is blocking the loop, so requests wait; it is a key health indicator for Node services.

topics.title: diagnostics_channel and Observability Hooks
topics.summary: A publish/subscribe channel built into Node that lets libraries emit diagnostics and tools observe them with no coupling.
topics.description:
**`diagnostics_channel`** is a lightweight, named publish/subscribe system. Libraries publish data on channels, and observability tools (APM, tracing, loggers) subscribe without patching the library.

### Why it exists
Before this, monitoring tools had to **monkey-patch** modules like `http` or `pg`. That is fragile. A channel offers an official, stable hook with almost zero cost when nobody subscribes.

### API
* `diagnostics_channel.channel('my.event')` get a channel object
* `channel.publish(data)` send a message
* `channel.subscribe((message, name) => ...)` / `unsubscribe`
* `channel.hasSubscribers` check before building expensive payloads
* `diagnostics_channel.subscribe(name, fn)` shortcut
* `tracingChannel(name)` publishes `start`, `end`, `asyncStart`, `asyncEnd` and `error` events around an operation

### Built-in channels
Node publishes channels for core modules, for example `http.client.request.start`, `http.server.request.start`, `net.client.socket`, and `undici:request:create` for fetch. Tools like OpenTelemetry, Datadog and Sentry subscribe to them.

### Related tools in the same family
| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| `AsyncLocalStorage` (`async_hooks`) | Per-request context (request id) across async calls |
| `perf_hooks` | Timing |
| `process.report`, `--heapsnapshot-signal` | Diagnostic reports and heap dumps |
| `v8.getHeapStatistics()` | Memory numbers |
| `inspector` | Programmatic debugger/profiler |

### Should you use it?
As an app developer you will mostly use it indirectly through APM tools. Library authors use it to expose events cleanly.

interview.q: What problem does diagnostics_channel solve?
interview.a: It gives libraries and Node core an official, low-overhead way to expose events (like HTTP requests starting) so monitoring tools can subscribe instead of monkey-patching modules.

interview.q: What is AsyncLocalStorage used for?
interview.a: To keep context, such as a request id or user, available throughout an asynchronous call chain without passing it through every function argument.
